title: Five Astronauts Just Sheltered for Evacuation on the Space Station. The Leak Is Getting Worse.
excerpt: A worsening air leak in the Russian Zvezda module forced NASA to order a two-hour safe-haven drill — the most serious safety incident on the ISS in years.
body:
Five astronauts aboard the International Space Station were ordered to take shelter in their SpaceX Crew Dragon spacecraft on Friday after a worsening air leak in the Russian segment of the station raised the possibility — however remote — of an emergency evacuation. It was the most serious safety incident on the ISS in recent memory, and it underscored the growing fragility of an orbital laboratory that has been continuously occupied for over 25 years.

NASA mission control at the Johnson Space Center in Houston issued the shelter-in-place order at 9:04 a.m. Eastern Time. The four members of SpaceX’s Crew-12 mission — NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev — along with NASA astronaut Chris Williams donned their spacesuits and entered the docked Crew Dragon Freedom capsule.

The order came as Russian cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikayev began what Roscosmos described as a “more extensive repair operation” on the Zvezda service module’s transfer tunnel, known as PrK. The tunnel, a small vestibule connecting Zvezda to a cargo docking port, has suffered from persistent cracks since engineers first detected air leaks in 2019. Despite multiple partial repairs over the years, the problem has never been fully resolved.

## The Leak Escalates

The air loss from Zvezda had been running at roughly one pound per day — concerning but manageable. On Friday, it escalated to two pounds per day, according to a senior NASA official who spoke on condition of anonymity. The jump prompted Roscosmos to attempt a more aggressive fix, reportedly involving the use of a saw to access the crack from a new angle.

NASA disagreed with the approach, according to the official, and ordered the safe-haven procedure as a precaution while the Russian repair was underway.

About two hours later, at approximately 11 a.m. ET, Roscosmos paused its repair work to gather additional measurements and data. NASA spokesperson Bethany Stevens then directed the crew to end safe-haven procedures and return to normal operations.

“We look forward to working with Roscosmos on a collaborative approach to address the leaks,” Stevens said in a statement posted on X.

## An Aging Station Under Pressure

The incident highlights a growing tension at the heart of the ISS program. Zvezda was installed in July 2000 as the first fully Russian contribution to the station. Its air leaks, while not new, are part of a broader pattern of aging infrastructure that NASA and Roscosmos have struggled to address cooperatively.

The ISS is currently home to seven people from two separate missions. Astronauts have never had to evacuate the station in its 27-year history, but Friday’s events brought that scenario closer to reality than it has been in years.

Legislation now before the U.S. Congress would extend the station’s operational life by two years, to 2032, giving commercial companies additional time to develop a replacement. The bill has bipartisan backing from Senator Ted Cruz and Senator Maria Cantwell, driven in part by concern over China’s growing capabilities in space — Beijing now operates its own Tiangong station independently.

## India’s Growing Stake in Space

The ISS drama carries particular resonance for India, which has been expanding its space ambitions at a rapid clip. ISRO’s successful Chandrayaan-3 lunar landing in 2023 made India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon, and the agency’s Gaganyaan crewed mission program is in advanced development.

India signed the Artemis Accords in 2023, aligning itself with the NASA-led framework for lunar exploration. As the ISS nears the end of its operational life, India — alongside Japan, the UAE, and private sector partners — is positioning itself as a key participant in whatever comes next, whether that is a commercial successor station or the Lunar Gateway.

For the Indian diaspora, which includes a significant number of aerospace engineers and scientists working at NASA, SpaceX, and other U.S. space organizations, the ISS remains a shared institutional asset. Indian-American astronaut Sunita Williams has logged over 322 days aboard the station across two missions.

## What Comes Next

The immediate concern is whether Roscosmos can develop a durable fix for the Zvezda leaks. NASA has been cautious in its public statements, but the agency’s decision to override Russia’s repair approach and order a safe-haven procedure speaks to the depth of the disagreement between the two programs.

The station’s air supply is not in immediate danger — the ISS has reserves and resupply capability. But a leak rate that doubles in a single day is not a trend anyone wants to see continue. For a structure that was never designed to last this long, every crack is a reminder that the clock is running.
